items.title: Blockbuster could have bought Netflix for $50 million in 2000
items.claim: In 2000, Netflix was a struggling DVD-by-mail service. What did Blockbuster's CEO John Antioco do when Reed Hastings flew to Dallas to propose a sale?

options.text: Agreed in principle but the deal collapsed over terms
Laughed Hastings out of the room
Counter-offered to buy Netflix for $200 million
Bought a minority stake to monitor the technology

items.reveal_title: The room where it didn't happen
items.reveal:
Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph have both told the story (Randolph's book 'That Will Never Work' has the most colour). They proposed Blockbuster acquire Netflix for $50 million and run blockbuster.com as the online arm. Antioco — facing a profitable late-fee business model — declined.

Blockbuster did later launch an online service (Blockbuster Online) and was on a recovery path under Antioco, but a 2005 boardroom fight with activist investor Carl Icahn led to Antioco's departure and the strategy's reversal. Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010.

Netflix's market cap is now over $300 billion.
items.why: Disruption isn't usually about technology incumbents can't access; it's about business models they can't bring themselves to attack. Late fees were too profitable to risk.

items.title: Just-in-time becomes a vulnerability under shock
items.claim: Toyota pioneered just-in-time inventory. What happened to Toyota production during the 2011 Tohoku earthquake?

options.text: Toyota's global production fell by around 800,000 vehicles because a single supplier of microcontrollers (Renesas) was damaged

items.reveal:
Renesas's Naka factory in Ibaraki produced ~30% of automotive microcontrollers globally. After the 11 March 2011 earthquake, Toyota's worldwide output dropped sharply through to mid-2011. After Tohoku, Toyota mandated suppliers to map upstream dependencies and hold buffer stocks for critical components — partially abandoning pure JIT.

The 2020-22 COVID semiconductor shortages repeated the lesson industry-wide.
items.why: Lean optimises against ordinary variation. It does not optimise against catastrophic disruption — and the same firms that pioneered it have had to add 'just-in-case' buffers.

items.title: Accounting profit and economic profit measure different things
items.claim: A bakery reports £80,000 accounting profit. The owner could earn £50,000 in alternative employment and £15,000 by renting out the premises. What is the economic profit?
items.reveal:
Accounting profit deducts only explicit costs. Economic profit also deducts opportunity costs — the next-best foregone returns to the owner's time and assets. Here: £80,000 - £50,000 - £15,000 = £15,000.

A business with positive accounting profit but negative economic profit is destroying value relative to alternatives. The distinction was formalised by Alfred Marshall in his 'Principles of Economics' (1890).
items.why: A firm reporting profit on its income statement may still be the wrong use of the owner's resources. Accounting standards weren't designed to answer that question.
